what_it_does: When AI chips run computations on sparse data — data with lots of zeros that can be skipped — they need to decide in advance how to chunk ('tile') that data into pieces that fit in the chip's small, fast on-chip memory. This paper tackles the problem that simple, fixed chunking strategies miss opportunities because the density of non-zero values varies across different parts of the data, while fully flexible strategies are too complicated to build. HYTE (Hybrid Static-Dynamic Tiling) uses a two-phase approach: before the chip runs, it samples a small portion of the data to pick a good initial chunking plan; then, as the chip actually runs, it fine-tunes chunk shapes on the fly to keep memory as full as possible. It also handles the bookkeeping overhead of tracking which values are non-zero — something earlier approaches overlooked.
